questions.title: Correct statement about bile acids
questions.question: A 56-year-old man has postprandial diarrhoea since an ileal resection and the surgeon suspects bile-acid malabsorption. Which statement about bile acids is correct?

options.B: The majority of bile acids is absorbed by passive diffusion
options.C: Glycine conjugates are more soluble than taurine conjugates
options.D: The amount lost in the stool each day represents the daily loss of cholesterol
options.E: The bile acid-dependent fraction of bile is stimulated by secretin

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bile salts are amphipathic and, especially when conjugated, quite water-soluble; that solubility is central to fat digestion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Most bile acids are reclaimed by active, sodium-dependent transport in the terminal ileum, not by passive diffusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Taurine conjugates are more water-soluble than glycine conjugates, not the reverse.
explanations.D: Correct. Only small amounts of bile acids escape the enterohepatic circulation into the stool each day, but this faecal loss is the body's only route for eliminating cholesterol, from which bile acids are synthesised. Conserving bile acids is therefore tightly coupled to cholesterol balance. Interrupting their reabsorption (ileal resection) increases this loss and lowers plasma cholesterol.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The bile acid-dependent fraction of bile is driven by the returning bile-acid pool, not by secretin, which stimulates the bicarbonate-rich (bile acid-independent) fraction.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 348, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that daily faecal loss of bile acids is the only route of cholesterol elimination and that conjugated bile salts are water-soluble.

questions.title: Feature distinguishing osmotic from secretory diarrhoea
questions.question: A 14-year-old ballerina has chronic diarrhoea that improves when she fasts; she drinks skim milk and denies laxatives. In contrast to secretory diarrhoea, which statement is correct about osmotic diarrhoea?

options.A: It is characterised by an increase in the stool osmotic gap
options.B: It is the result of increased crypt cell secretion
options.C: It is the result of decreased electroneutral sodium absorption
options.D: It is caused by bacterial toxins
options.E: It occurs only in the colon

explanations.A: Correct. Osmotic diarrhoea occurs when poorly absorbed, osmotically active solutes draw water into the lumen, so the stool osmotic gap is increased. It characteristically ceases with fasting or on stopping the offending solute, as here. Common causes are lactase deficiency, magnesium salts and non-absorbable sugars.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased crypt-cell secretion of an isosmotic chloride solution is the mechanism of secretory, not osmotic, diarrhoea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inhibited electroneutral NaCl absorption underlies secretory diarrhoea; the stool gap there is normal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bacterial toxins typically cause secretory diarrhoea, which does not stop with fasting.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osmotic diarrhoea arises from unabsorbed solute in the small intestine or colon, not the colon alone.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 349, correct = a) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that osmotic diarrhoea raises the stool osmotic gap and stops with fasting, unlike secretory diarrhoea.

questions.title: Segment where short-chain fatty acids are absorbed
questions.question: An 83-year-old woman with constipation is given a high-fibre diet, raising production of short-chain fatty acids. Short-chain fatty acid absorption occurs almost exclusively from which segment of the gut?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stomach neither generates nor absorbs short-chain fatty acids.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The duodenum is a site of digestion of dietary fat, not of colonic short-chain fatty acid absorption.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The jejunum absorbs digested nutrients but is not the site of short-chain fatty acid uptake.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ileum reabsorbs bile salts and vitamin B12, not the bacterially generated short-chain fatty acids.
explanations.E: Correct. Short-chain fatty acids are products of colonic bacterial fermentation of undigested carbohydrate, and the colon is the major site for both their generation and their absorption. They also exert trophic effects on the colonic mucosa and promote colonic sodium absorption.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 351, correct = e) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that short-chain fatty acids are generated and absorbed in the colon and support colonic sodium absorption and mucosal growth.

questions.title: Correct statement about GI water and electrolyte absorption
questions.question: A patient has vomiting and severe watery diarrhoea after spoiled shellfish and stool is positive for Vibrio cholerae. Which statement best describes water and electrolyte absorption in the gut?

options.A: Most water and electrolytes come from ingested fluids
options.B: The small intestine and colon have similar absorptive capacities
options.C: Osmotic equilibration of chyme occurs in the stomach
options.D: The majority of absorption occurs in the jejunum
options.E: Cholera toxin inhibits sodium-coupled nutrient transport

explanations.A: Incorrect. Most of the 9-12 litres handled daily comes from gastrointestinal secretions, not ingested fluid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The small intestine absorbs far more fluid than the colon, whose capacity is limited to a few litres per day.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osmotic equilibration of chyme occurs in the duodenum, not the stomach.
explanations.D: Correct. Most water and electrolyte absorption occurs in the jejunum, with the duodenum equilibrating chyme osmotically. Water follows passively the active absorption of sodium. The colon reclaims only a small remaining fraction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cholera toxin drives secretion by raising cyclic AMP; crucially it does not impair sodium-coupled glucose transport, which is why oral rehydration therapy works.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 356, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that most gut water absorption is in the jejunum, driven passively by active sodium absorption, with the colon reclaiming a small fraction.

questions.title: Mechanism of symptoms in dumping syndrome
questions.question: After a jejunum-to-stomach anastomosis a patient has post-meal weakness, dizziness and sweating. The symptoms of dumping syndrome are caused in part by which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood pressure tends to fall, not rise, as fluid shifts into the gut.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucagon excess is not the mechanism of dumping symptoms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholecystokinin release is not the cause of the weakness, dizziness and sweating.
explanations.D: Correct. When the stomach's reservoir and control of emptying are lost, a hypertonic meal enters the intestine rapidly. This drives a large insulin surge that produces reactive hypoglycaemia, causing weakness, dizziness and sweating. Rapid osmotic movement of water into the gut also causes hypovolaemia and hypotension.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Although an early glucose spike can occur, the symptomatic component highlighted here is the subsequent reactive hypoglycaemia, not sustained hyperglycaemia.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 363, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: Explain that loss of gastric reservoir function delivers a hypertonic load rapidly, causing reactive hypoglycaemia and fluid shifts in dumping syndrome.

questions.title: Diagnosis with elevated direct-acting bilirubin
questions.question: A patient is found to have elevated levels of direct-acting (conjugated) plasma bilirubin. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Obstruction of the common bile duct

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tropical sprue causes malabsorption, not a predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Terminal ileal bypass causes bile-acid and fat malabsorption, not conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pancreatitis need not raise conjugated bilirubin unless it obstructs the bile duct; it is not the best answer here.
explanations.D: Correct. When bilirubin has already been conjugated in the liver but cannot be excreted, as in common bile duct obstruction, the conjugated (direct) fraction is reabsorbed into blood and rises. This post-hepatic pattern contrasts with the mixed rise of hepatocellular disease. Alkaline phosphatase typically rises with it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bile reflux gastropathy irritates the gastric mucosa and does not cause conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 367, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that common bile duct obstruction raises conjugated (direct) bilirubin, the post-hepatic jaundice pattern.

questions.title: Major mechanism of sodium absorption in the small intestine
questions.question: Which of the following is the major mechanism for absorption of sodium from the small intestine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Na+-H+ exchange is one component but, on its own, is not the major mechanism named here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sodium is not absorbed by cotransport with potassium in the small intestine.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Electrogenic sodium transport predominates in the colon, not as the major small-intestinal route.
explanations.D: Correct. Sodium absorption is the primary absorptive event of the small intestine and drives the uptake of water and other electrolytes. Its major mechanism is neutral NaCl absorption, coupling Na+-H+ exchange with Cl--HCO3- exchange so that no net charge moves. Nutrient-coupled and other pathways contribute additionally.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Solvent drag carries some sodium with absorbed water but is not the major mechanism.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 368, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that neutral NaCl absorption (coupled Na+-H+ and Cl--HCO3- exchange) is the major mechanism of small-intestinal sodium absorption.

questions.title: Major protection of the duodenal mucosa from gastric acid
questions.question: A 33-year-old woman on large doses of NSAIDs has burning epigastric pain that improves after meals, suggesting a duodenal ulcer. What is the major factor protecting the duodenal mucosa from damage by gastric acid?

options.B: The endogenous mucosal barrier of the duodenum

explanations.A: Correct. Unlike the stomach, the duodenal mucosa has little endogenous barrier of its own, so it depends on neutralisation of the acid delivered to it. Acid entering the duodenum releases secretin, which drives pancreatic bicarbonate secretion; this pancreatic output matches gastric acid output and neutralises it. It is therefore the major protective factor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The duodenum lacks the substantial endogenous mucosal barrier that protects the stomach, so this is not the major factor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Duodenal (Brunner gland) bicarbonate contributes but is minor compared with the large pancreatic bicarbonate output.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The liver's bicarbonate contribution is small and not the principal neutraliser.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bile contains some bicarbonate but not in amounts sufficient to neutralise gastric acid.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 371, correct = a) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that secretin-driven pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is the major factor neutralising acid and protecting the duodenal mucosa.
